meta.basis: worldwide consumer spending on video games, nominal US dollars
meta.note: Quarterly values are modelled from annual research using segment seasonality and platform launch quarters. No public quarterly series exists before ~2010. See research/RESEARCH-NOTES.md.

ranges.note: Reconstructed from trade-press unit estimates; no market research existed yet.
Play Meter / Vending Times arcade surveys and contemporaneous retail estimates.
US retail well covered; Japan from Capcom/Sega IR; Europe estimated.
NPD/DFC/Enterbrain coverage is good for retail, weaker for online and China.
Newzoo, Sensor Tower and company filings; 2026 is a forecast.

platforms.label: Magnavox Odyssey
platforms.note: The first home console. Sold ~350,000 units; games were plastic overlays taped to the TV.

platforms.label: Dedicated Pong consoles
platforms.note: Atari Home Pong, Coleco Telstar, Sears Tele-Games and ~80 imitators. One-chip machines with games built in; the market collapsed in 1977–78 when cartridges arrived.

platforms.label: Atari 2600 (VCS)
platforms.note: The console that made cartridges normal. ~30M sold; still shipping in 1992 as the cut-price "2600 Jr".

platforms.label: Mattel Intellivision
platforms.note: Marketed with George Plimpton ads that lined its graphics up against the Atari 2600 — the first console "console war".

platforms.label: ColecoVision
platforms.note: Shipped with a near-arcade-perfect Donkey Kong. Coleco abandoned it in 1985 to make Cabbage Patch Kids dolls.

platforms.label: NES / Famicom
platforms.note: 61.9M sold with 500M games. Nintendo's lockout chip and licence terms — five games a year, Nintendo manufactures the carts — rebuilt an industry that retailers had written off.

platforms.label: Sega Master System
platforms.note: A distant second in the US and Japan, but a genuine phenomenon in Brazil, where Tectoy still sold new units into the 2010s.

platforms.label: Mega Drive / Genesis
platforms.note: Sega of America's "Genesis does what Nintendon't" campaign took Sega to roughly half the US 16-bit market by 1993 — the closest anyone came to beating Nintendo in that era.

platforms.label: PC Engine / TurboGrafx-16
platforms.note: Briefly outsold the Famicom in Japan. Its CD-ROM² add-on (1988) was the first CD games console anywhere.

platforms.label: Neo Geo AES
platforms.note: A literal arcade board for the living room, at $649 with $200 cartridges. Tiny install base, enormous revenue per owner.

platforms.label: CD-i, 3DO & CD32
platforms.note: The $699 3DO and the $700 CD-i tried to sell "multimedia" instead of games. Both are cautionary tales about pricing a console like a VCR.

platforms.label: Sega Saturn
platforms.note: Sega surprise-launched it in the US four months early, at $399 against the PlayStation's $299. Retailers who had been cut out of the launch never forgave them.

platforms.label: PlayStation
platforms.note: Sony's first console shipped 102.5M units and 962M games. CDs cost cents to press against $20+ for a cartridge, which is most of why third-party publishers switched sides.

platforms.label: Nintendo 64
platforms.note: Nintendo stayed on cartridges for speed and piracy control. It cost them Final Fantasy VII — and with it, Japan.

platforms.label: Sega Dreamcast
platforms.note: First console with a built-in modem and online play as standard. Sega quit the hardware business in January 2001, 16 months after launch.

platforms.label: PlayStation 2
platforms.note: The best-selling console ever: ~155M units, 1.54B games, and 13 years on the market. It was also the cheapest DVD player in Japan at launch.

platforms.label: Xbox
platforms.note: The first console built around an integrated ethernet port. Xbox Live (2002) turned paid online multiplayer into an industry default.

platforms.label: Xbox 360
platforms.note: Launched a year ahead of Sony and led the US for most of the generation, despite a hardware failure rate that cost Microsoft $1.15B in warranty extensions.

platforms.label: Nintendo Wii
platforms.note: Motion control sold 101.6M consoles to people who had never bought one before. Wii Sports alone shipped 82.9M copies.

platforms.label: PlayStation 3
platforms.note: Launched at $499/$599 — Sony lost roughly $250 on every unit — and shipped with a Blu-ray drive that won the format war for them.

platforms.label: Wii U
platforms.note: Nintendo's worst-selling home console at 13.6M. Almost its entire library was later re-sold, profitably, on Switch.

platforms.label: PlayStation 4
platforms.note: 117.2M units. This is the generation where digital passed physical and where in-game spending — season passes, battle passes, cosmetics — became the majority of console software revenue.

platforms.label: Xbox One
platforms.note: A Kinect-bundled $499 launch and a mishandled always-online message put Microsoft behind by roughly 2:1. Game Pass (2017) was the strategic answer.

platforms.label: Nintendo Switch
platforms.note: A hybrid that made the home/handheld split obsolete. 156M units — Nintendo's best-selling system — and Nintendo never once cut the $299 launch price.

platforms.label: PlayStation 5
platforms.note: Supply-constrained for two full years by the semiconductor shortage. Sony then raised the price rather than cutting it — across Europe, Japan and Canada in August 2022, and in Europe again in April 2025. Mid-generation price rises had essentially never happened before.

platforms.label: Xbox Series X|S
platforms.note: Microsoft stopped reporting console sales in 2022 and now publishes its games on PlayStation and Switch. The $69B Activision Blizzard deal closed in October 2023.

platforms.label: Nintendo Switch 2
platforms.note: Launched 5 June 2025 and sold ~10.4M units in under four months — the fastest console start ever recorded.

platforms.label: Game & Watch
platforms.note: Single-game LCD units, 43.4M sold. They funded the R&D that became the Game Boy, and gave it the D-pad.

platforms.label: Game Boy & Game Boy Color
platforms.note: A monochrome screen and a worse CPU than its rivals, but 10–30 hours on four AA batteries. Tetris made it a commuter device; Pokémon (1996 JP, 1998 worldwide) doubled its sales seven years into its life.

platforms.label: Sega Game Gear
platforms.note: Colour screen, six AA batteries, three to five hours. The Game Boy won on battery life.

platforms.label: Nokia N-Gage
platforms.note: A phone you held sideways against your ear to talk. Sold ~3M against a 6M first-year target.

platforms.label: Nintendo DS
platforms.note: 154M units — the best-selling handheld ever. Two screens, a stylus and Brain Age pulled in an audience that did not think of itself as gamers.

platforms.label: PlayStation Portable
platforms.note: 80M units and a genuine hit in Japan, where Monster Hunter Portable 3rd sold 4.9M copies domestically.

platforms.label: Nintendo 3DS
platforms.note: Launched at $249 to poor reviews and was cut to $169 within five months — Nintendo's fastest price cut ever, and the moment it became clear phones had taken the casual handheld market.

platforms.label: PlayStation Vita
platforms.note: Sony's last handheld. Proprietary memory cards cost more than the games; it sold ~16M and was discontinued in 2019.

platforms.label: Atari (arcade)
platforms.note: Pong (1972), Breakout (1976), Asteroids (1979), Missile Command, Centipede, Tempest. Atari built the arcade business and then, in 1983, nearly ended it.

platforms.label: Taito
platforms.note: Space Invaders (1978) grossed roughly $2bn in coin drop and is often credited with a nationwide 100-yen coin shortage in Japan — a story that is probably a myth, but the machines were real enough.

platforms.label: Namco / Bandai Namco
platforms.note: Pac-Man (1980) sold ~100,000 cabinets in the US alone and took over $1bn in quarters in its first year. Namco still runs Japan's largest arcade chain.

platforms.label: Sega (arcade)
platforms.note: Out Run (1986), After Burner, Virtua Fighter (1993), Daytona USA (1994). Sega's Model 2 and Model 3 boards kept arcades ahead of home consoles until roughly 1999 — after that, they weren't.

platforms.label: Nintendo (arcade)
platforms.note: Donkey Kong (1981) was designed by a first-time director named Shigeru Miyamoto after a Radar Scope conversion failed. It made Nintendo's US arm solvent.

platforms.label: Midway / Bally / Williams
platforms.note: Midway licensed Space Invaders and Pac-Man for the US, then made Defender (1980), Mortal Kombat (1992) and NBA Jam (1993) — the last of which took roughly $1bn in its first year.

platforms.label: Konami (arcade)
platforms.note: Frogger (1981), Gradius, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (1989) and then Dance Dance Revolution (1998), which kept Japanese arcades alive by making them a place you went to be watched.

platforms.label: Capcom (arcade)
platforms.note: Street Fighter II (1991) is the highest-grossing arcade game ever made: over $10.6bn in coin drop across its revisions. It also invented the competitive fighting-game scene.

platforms.label: Boxed retail
platforms.note: Software in a cardboard box on a shelf. It was effectively the whole PC market until Battle.net and Steam, and it is now a rounding error — under 0.1% of PC spending.

platforms.label: Valve — Steam
platforms.note: Steam launched in 2003 as a mandatory patcher for Counter-Strike, and players hated it. It is now the default PC storefront: >130M monthly users, a 30% cut, and an estimated $11.1bn of gross sales in the first half of 2026 alone.

platforms.label: Blizzard — Battle.net
platforms.note: World of Warcraft peaked at 12 million subscribers in 2010 and was, for years, the largest single revenue source in PC gaming. Its $15/month price became the reference for every subscription that followed. (Blizzard's boxed sales before 2004 sit in the retail band.)

platforms.label: Nexon / NCSoft — Korean portals
platforms.note: Lineage (1998) and MapleStory (2003) invented free-to-play with an item shop years before the West accepted it. Korea also built the PC bang — the internet café as a paid venue — which is why Korean online games were billed by the hour long before anyone else sold cosmetics.

platforms.label: Tencent — WeGame & China PC
platforms.note: CrossFire and Dungeon & Fighter were, for most of the 2010s, two of the three highest-grossing games on Earth — almost entirely inside China, and almost invisible to Western coverage of the industry.

platforms.label: Riot — Riot client
platforms.note: League of Legends (2009) made free-to-play respectable in the West by selling only cosmetics — no paid power. Riot has been wholly owned by Tencent since 2015; it is shown separately because it publishes through its own client.

platforms.label: Browser & social games
platforms.note: Flash portals, then Facebook. FarmVille had 83 million monthly players in 2010. Adobe ended Flash support on 31 December 2020 and most of this catalogue simply stopped existing.

platforms.label: Epic — EGS & Fortnite
platforms.note: Fortnite made an estimated $5.4bn across all platforms in 2018. The Epic Games Store opened that December taking 12% instead of Steam's 30%, and bought timed exclusives with the difference.

platforms.label: Microsoft — Store & PC Game Pass
platforms.note: Minecraft sold direct from a website before any storefront would carry it; Microsoft bought Mojang for $2.5bn in 2014. PC Game Pass followed in 2019. (Microsoft's boxed PC games before 2011 sit in the retail band.)

platforms.label: EA — Origin & EA App
platforms.note: EA pulled its games off Steam in 2011 to launch Origin, then quietly put them back in 2019. Only what is bought inside EA's own client counts here.

platforms.label: Feature-phone & carrier decks
platforms.note: Snake shipped on 400 million Nokia handsets from 1997. Japan's i-mode and the US carrier decks then built a $3–4bn/yr Java and BREW games business that the App Store erased in about four years.

platforms.label: King / Activision
platforms.note: Candy Crush Saga (2012) was making around $1.5bn a year at peak and is still a top-10 grosser more than a decade later. Activision Blizzard bought King for $5.9bn in 2015.

platforms.label: Supercell
platforms.note: Clash of Clans (2012) and Brawl Stars from a studio of a few hundred people. Tencent bought a controlling stake in 2016 at an $8.6bn valuation.

platforms.label: Tencent (mobile)
platforms.note: Honor of Kings has been the highest-grossing mobile game in the world for most of the last decade — roughly $2bn a year, almost all of it inside China. PUBG Mobile added a second global hit in 2018.

platforms.label: Niantic
platforms.note: Pokémon GO hit 500 million downloads within two months of its July 2016 launch and has taken over $8bn since. Scopely bought Niantic's games business for $3.5bn in 2025.

platforms.label: HoYoverse
platforms.note: Genshin Impact (2020) took roughly $1bn on mobile in its first six months and proved a console-quality free-to-play game could be self-published globally from China.

platforms.label: Zynga / Take-Two
platforms.note: Take-Two bought Zynga in 2022 in a deal announced at $12.7bn. Monopoly Go, launched in 2023, passed $3bn in player spending in under two years.

platforms.label: Sea / Garena
platforms.note: Free Fire was built deliberately for cheap Android handsets and slow connections, which is why it became the biggest mobile shooter in Brazil, India and South-East Asia while barely registering in the US.

platforms.label: Dream Games
platforms.note: A studio founded in Istanbul in 2019 whose single game, Royal Match, now out-earns most publicly listed games companies.

platforms.label: Aniplex (Sony)
platforms.note: Fate/Grand Order is a text-heavy gacha game that has taken over $6bn, almost all of it in Japan — the clearest example of a mobile hit that is invisible outside its home market.

platforms.label: Oculus Rift & Rift S
platforms.note: The Kickstarter (2012) that restarted VR. Facebook bought Oculus for $2bn in 2014, two years before the Rift shipped.

platforms.label: Meta Quest
platforms.note: Quest 2 (2020) was the first standalone headset to sell in the tens of millions. Quest store content revenue passed $1bn in Feb 2021, $2bn in Sep 2023 and ~$3bn by Mar 2025 — steady, but not the growth curve Meta wanted.

platforms.label: PlayStation VR
platforms.note: PSVR1 sold ~5M units on the back of an installed base of 100M+ PS4s. PSVR2 (2023) shipped 1.7M in its launch year and then fell to ~0.8M in 2024.

platforms.label: Valve Index & SteamVR
platforms.note: Half-Life: Alyx (2020) is still the only true system-seller VR has produced; Index headsets sold out worldwide for months around its launch.

platforms.label: Apple Vision Pro
platforms.note: A $3,499 "spatial computer" that Apple pointedly did not market as a games device. Its games catalogue remains small.

platforms.label: Sony (PS Now / Plus Premium)
platforms.note: Sony bought Gaikai for $380M in 2012 and OnLive's patents in 2015. PS Now was the highest-earning cloud service in the world as late as 2021, largely because nobody else had scale.

platforms.label: Microsoft (Xbox Cloud Gaming)
platforms.note: xCloud is bundled into Game Pass Ultimate rather than sold on its own, which is why its true revenue is an allocation rather than a line item.

platforms.label: NVIDIA GeForce Now
platforms.note: The only major service that streams games you already own, rather than a catalogue it licenses.

platforms.label: Google Stadia
platforms.note: Launched November 2019, stopped funding first-party development in February 2021, shut down 18 January 2023. Google refunded every hardware and software purchase.

platforms.label: Other arcade makers
platforms.note: Data East, Irem, Jaleco, Nichibutsu, Technos, Atari Games post-1985, Raw Thrills, and the modern redemption/ticket operators that now make up most of Western arcade floor space.

platforms.label: Other stores & direct sales
platforms.note: GOG, itch.io, Ubisoft Connect, Battle-net-era Chinese operators (Shanda, Giant, Perfect World, Changyou), Roblox on PC, and every developer selling straight from their own site.

platforms.label: Other mobile publishers
platforms.note: Several thousand publishers — hypercasual studios, the Chinese third-party Android stores, and a very long tail of gacha and puzzle games. Mobile is the least concentrated segment in gaming: even after naming the nineteen largest publishers, roughly half of all spending still sits in this band.

platforms.label: Other VR
platforms.note: Samsung Gear VR and Google Cardboard/Daydream (huge in units, negligible in revenue), Windows Mixed Reality, Pimax, Varjo, Bigscreen and the location-based VR arcades.

platforms.label: Other cloud services
platforms.note: Shadow, Boosteroid, Blacknut, and the large Chinese services (Tencent Start, Huawei Cloud Game, migu) that operate almost entirely inside China.

events.title: The first arcade video game goes on sale
events.text: Nutting Associates ships 1,500 Computer Space cabinets. It flops — players find the controls incomprehensible — but its designers, Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney, found Atari the following year.

events.title: Pong, and the first home console
events.text: Atari's Pong turns coin-op video games into a business. The same year Magnavox ships the Odyssey, the first home console: no CPU, no software, just circuits and plastic overlays you taped to your TV.

events.title: Home Pong at Sears
events.text: Sears sells Atari's Home Pong exclusively for one Christmas and orders 150,000 units. Within two years roughly 80 companies are selling near-identical one-chip Pong boxes, and the market crashes.

events.title: The Atari 2600 makes games a catalogue
events.text: Interchangeable cartridges mean the console is no longer the product — the library is. About 30 million 2600s were eventually sold, and it stayed on shelves until 1992.

events.title: Space Invaders
events.text: Taito's game takes an estimated $2 billion in coin drop and single-handedly triples the size of the Japanese arcade market. Japanese operators open venues that stock nothing else.

events.title: Pac-Man earns over $1 billion in quarters
events.text: Namco's maze game sells around 100,000 cabinets in the US alone in its first year. A good machine took $200–240 a week; the best took $800.

events.title: Game & Watch
events.text: Nintendo starts selling single-game LCD handhelds designed by Gunpei Yokoi. 43.4 million sold, and the D-pad invented for Donkey Kong (1982) is still the standard control today.

events.title: Donkey Kong saves Nintendo of America
events.text: Nintendo's US arm is sitting on 2,000 unsold Radar Scope cabinets. A first-time game director, Shigeru Miyamoto, converts them into Donkey Kong. It sells 60,000 units.

events.title: Peak arcade
events.text: US arcades take somewhere between $5 and $8 billion in quarters, depending on whose survey you believe — comparable to the entire US box office and the recorded-music business put together.

events.title: The crash of 1983
events.text: North American console revenue falls by roughly 97% over two years. The causes: too many machines, unlicensed shovelware, and retailers who would no longer take the inventory risk. Atari buries unsold E.T. cartridges in a New Mexico landfill.

events.title: Famicom launches in Japan
events.text: Nintendo sells the Family Computer for ¥14,800 — cheaper than any competitor — and takes a manufacturing margin on every licensed cartridge instead. That model funds the next twenty years.

events.title: The NES reopens American retail
events.text: Nintendo test-markets the NES in New York with a robot, a light gun and a money-back guarantee, because "video game" was a word toy buyers refused to hear. National rollout follows in 1986.

events.title: Game Boy, bundled with Tetris
events.text: A monochrome screen and a weaker chip than its rivals, but 10–30 hours on four AA batteries. Bundling Tetris aimed it at adults as much as children. 118.7 million sold across Game Boy and Game Boy Color.

events.title: "Genesis does what Nintendon't"
events.text: Sega of America attacks Nintendo by name — unheard of in games advertising — and takes roughly half the US 16-bit market by 1993. It is the only time anyone seriously threatened Nintendo at home.

events.title: Street Fighter II
events.text: Capcom's fighter has taken over $10.6 billion in coin drop across its revisions — the highest-grossing arcade game ever made. It also created competitive fighting games as a scene.

events.title: Doom, and shareware distribution
events.text: id Software gives away the first episode and sells the rest by mail order, bypassing retail entirely. Within two years Doom is estimated to be installed on more PCs than Windows 95.

events.title: PlayStation and the switch to CDs
events.text: Sony enters the market after Nintendo walks away from a joint CD-ROM project. A CD costs cents to press; a cartridge costs $20+. Third-party publishers move en masse.

events.title: Pokémon Red and Green
events.text: Released on a Game Boy everyone assumed was finished, seven years into its life. Handheld revenue roughly doubles between 1995 and 1999 on the back of it.

events.title: Snake ships on 400 million phones
events.text: Nokia preloads Snake on the 6110. It is not sold and earns nothing directly, but it is the first time hundreds of millions of people carry a game in their pocket.

events.title: Lineage and the item shop
events.text: NCSoft launches Lineage in Korea. Korean studios spend the next decade proving that free-to-play with paid items out-earns box sales — years before Western publishers accept it.

events.title: Dreamcast ships with a modem
events.text: Sega puts a 56k modem in every unit and runs online play as standard. It sells 9.1 million and Sega leaves the hardware business in January 2001, 16 months after the US launch.

events.title: PlayStation 2 — 155 million units
events.text: The best-selling console ever made, on sale for 13 years. In Japan it was also, briefly, the cheapest DVD player you could buy, which is why it sold out in three days.

events.title: The Sims
events.text: Will Wright's game about domestic life sells to an audience that is roughly half women, at a time when the industry assumed it did not have one. It becomes the best-selling PC franchise of its era.

events.title: Xbox, with an ethernet port
events.text: Microsoft ships the first console with integrated broadband networking. Xbox Live follows in November 2002 and makes paid online multiplayer a normal thing to charge for.

events.title: Steam
events.text: Valve launches Steam as a mandatory patcher for Counter-Strike and is widely loathed for it. Twenty years later it is the default PC storefront, taking a 30% cut of most of the segment.

events.title: World of Warcraft
events.text: Peaks at 12 million subscribers in 2010. For most of a decade a single game is the largest revenue line in PC gaming, and the $15/month subscription becomes the reference price for everything.

events.title: Nintendo DS and PSP arrive together
events.text: Two screens and a stylus against a machine that plays UMD movies. The DS ends up at 154 million units — the best-selling handheld ever — and the PSP at 80 million. Handheld revenue peaks in 2007.

events.title: Wii, PS3 and the price of ambition
events.text: Sony launches the PS3 at $499/$599, losing an estimated $250 a unit. Nintendo launches the Wii at $249 with motion control and sells 101.6 million — largely to people who had never bought a console.

events.title: iPhone
events.text: No games at launch and no third-party apps at all. The App Store arrives in July 2008 with a 70/30 split and no gatekeeper beyond review — the lowest barrier to publishing a game that had ever existed.

events.title: The App Store, and the collapse of the $50 game
events.text: Within two years the going rate for a mobile game falls from $9.99 to $0.99 to free. The dominant business model shifts from selling a copy to selling to the small fraction of players who spend.

events.title: FarmVille and League of Legends
events.text: Two free-to-play launches within months of each other: one on Facebook, peaking at 83 million monthly players, one on PC. Only one of them still exists.

events.title: Minecraft leaves beta
events.text: Sold direct from a website, by a studio of a handful of people, before any storefront would carry it. Microsoft buys Mojang for $2.5 billion in 2014; it is now the best-selling game of all time.

events.title: Candy Crush and Clash of Clans
events.text: Two 2012 launches that make free-to-play the default. Both were still top-grossing titles more than ten years later; Activision Blizzard paid $5.9 billion for King in 2015.

events.title: GTA V takes $800 million in a day
events.text: And $1 billion in three. Its online mode then keeps earning for over a decade, which is the clearest early demonstration that a console game could be a service rather than a product.

events.title: China lifts its console ban
events.text: China's ban on console sales, in force since 2000, is lifted nationwide. It changes less than expected: the market had already been built around PC and mobile, and it stays there.

events.title: Pokémon GO
events.text: 500 million downloads within two months of its July launch, and over $8 billion in player spending since. It also proved a mobile game could be a physical, public event.

events.title: Consumer VR finally ships
events.text: Oculus Rift, HTC Vive and, that October, PlayStation VR. Sales are an order of magnitude below the forecasts, and VR settles in at 2–3% of industry revenue rather than replacing the screen.

events.title: Nintendo Switch
events.text: A hybrid that ends the home/handheld distinction Nintendo itself created. 156 million units, and Nintendo never cut the $299 launch price in eight years.

events.title: Fortnite Battle Royale
events.text: Added as a free mode two months after the paid game launched, and it took over. An estimated $5.4 billion in 2018 across platforms, and the battle pass replaces the loot box as the industry's default.

events.title: The Epic Games Store opens at 12%
events.text: Epic undercuts Steam's 30% cut by more than half and buys timed exclusives with the difference. Steam's share barely moves, but the 30% standard is now permanently contested.

events.title: Stadia launches
events.text: Google promises games with no console at all. It stops funding its own studios 15 months later and shuts the service on 18 January 2023, refunding every purchase.

events.title: Lockdowns
events.text: Console spending jumps by a fifth in a single year while arcades close almost completely — arcade revenue roughly halves. It is the sharpest one-year divergence anywhere in this chart.

events.title: PS5 and Xbox Series launch into a chip shortage
events.text: Both are supply-constrained for two years. In August 2022 Sony raises the PS5 price across Europe, Japan and Canada — and again in Europe in 2025 — rather than cutting it. Mid-generation price rises had essentially never happened before.

events.title: Genshin Impact
events.text: A free, console-quality game self-published globally from Shanghai, taking roughly $1 billion on mobile in six months. It ends the assumption that Chinese studios need a Western partner.

events.title: Mobile passes half the industry
events.text: Mobile spending reaches $93 billion — more than PC and console combined. More than half of it comes from Asia-Pacific, and most of the top-grossing titles never chart in the West.

events.title: Microsoft bids $69 billion for Activision Blizzard
events.text: The largest acquisition in the history of the industry, roughly the size of the entire global games market in 2010. It closes in October 2023 after regulators in three jurisdictions try to block it.

events.title: Japanese arcades come back — smaller
events.text: Operating revenue recovers for a third straight year after the pandemic, but the floor is now mostly prize machines and rhythm games. Video-game coin drop never returns to its 2007 level.

events.title: The layoff year
events.text: More than 14,000 games jobs are cut in 2024 after two years of near-flat revenue. The industry stops growing faster than its costs.

events.title: Nintendo Switch 2
events.text: Launches 5 June 2025 at $449 and sells roughly 10.4 million units in under four months — the fastest start any console has had. Console is the fastest-growing segment of 2025 as a result.

events.title: Steam's biggest half-year
events.text: Games on Steam take an estimated $11.1 billion gross in the first half of 2026. Thirty years after PC gaming was written off as a dying platform, it is the segment growing most reliably.
